verdicts.reasoning: The statistics do not support the number. Observing zero money-bearing errors in 300 lines gives, by the rule of three, a 95% upper bound of about 1.0% on the escaped rate; demonstrating 0.5% or below at 95% confidence needs about 600 clean lines, and 'money-bearing' errors are rarer than all errors so the sample must be larger still. The digest itself lists 'a statistician should size N' as an open question and calls 200-500 a heuristic borrowed from medical-coding audits. Golden tests prove the code reproduces its own rules; they say nothing about wrong parameters, wrong primitives (a misread IL) or a preamble misread, which are where derived-line errors come from, and those errors are systematic across a family rather than independent per line, so a per-line rate understates exposure. Commercially, a wrong derived quantity in a tender feeds KKL's rates and resourcing (contractor's risk under PSSCOC), in a claim it is cut by the SO with credibility cost, and in a subcon certificate it puts KKL as SOP Act respondent with a 14 or 21-day response window and no right to raise reasons later (s.15(3)); none of this is protected by a 300-line record. Rulebook confirmation is a necessary gate; it is not an error-rate proof.

verdicts.reasoning: The local-geometry half is sound and is the right architecture. The text half is a legal conclusion nobody at KKL has yet made. Section 5 of the Official Secrets Act applies to persons who obtained a document under a contract with the Government and criminalises communicating it to an unauthorised person (fine and up to two years); BQ line text, preambles and schedules are the tender document, and on LTA contracts the tender documents are password-gated behind an NDA signed and stamped on every page. Whether transmitting that text to a US-processed API is an authorised communication depends on the NDA's third-party-processing and consent wording, which the digest lists as unread. Zero data retention with Anthropic is not a default: it is a per-organisation arrangement obtained through sales subject to approval, does not cover Batch (29-day retention) and is not available for Covered Models with 30-day retention; the standard API processes in the US, and a Singapore-resident route exists only via Bedrock in-region inference in ap-southeast-1 with a different data processor. The Infrastructure Protection Act point is stronger: for protected places such as MRT depots, 'photograph' includes drawings, plans and measurements, so rail drawings should not merely avoid cloud calls but need handling rules on KKL's own machines. Also the BQ with rates is KKL's most commercially sensitive document and the client's price schedule is confidential under GeBIZ tender conditions. 'Satisfies ... for most public-sector civil contracts' cannot be asserted from the evidence; 'is a defensible position to put to each client in writing' can.

overall:
The design leans hardest on five claims. C1 and C2 decide whether the rulebook spine is worth building at all: without a live Price Document count and three encoded preambles, the 60% share and the 40-parameter rulebook are guesses, and the Sentosa schedule already shows trench items that swallow the 'derived lines'. C8 and C13 carry the cash case: the claims module is sold as the largest recurring saving, but DR Capture only records chainage on drainage-structure rows and never on kerb, pavement or excavation rows, the SO certifies on joint measurement rather than daily reports, and the 25-30% hours share is the digest's own low-confidence inference. C9 gates everything that touches a cloud model: the Official Secrets Act reaches persons who obtained documents under a government contract, LTA tender documents sit behind an NDA signed on every page, zero data retention is a negotiated per-organisation arrangement rather than a default, and nobody at KKL has read the NDAs. C10 is the quiet failure: the six-month list is 16-17 person-weeks of work on an 8-13 person-week allocation, from a single builder who also keeps the site apps alive. C4 and C14 share one statistical flaw: 300 clean lines cannot demonstrate a 0.5% escaped-error rate (the 95% bound is about 1%), so the graduation gates as written would promote families on evidence that does not support the number KKL would be telling its SOs, subcontractors and insurer.

What the sceptic would change. First, spend the first two weeks on paper, not code: count three live BQs by line and by value, encode three preambles by hand, read five NDAs and write a per-client confidentiality position, pull last year's SO queries and subcon disputes to get KKL's real escaped-error rate, and run the two-week QS time log. Those six items cost under three person-weeks and settle C1, C2, C9, C12 and C13 before a builder-week is spent. Second, treat year one as a capped experiment with stop-loss reviews at months 3 and 6 and a cash conversion stated up front (deferred hire or extra tenders bid), because time banked as capacity is not a saving the finance head can book. Third, cut the six-month scope to engine, two rulebook families and the BQ binder, with the claims roll-up as a shadow compile script and the harvester conditional on the inbox sample; name a second maintainer by month 6. Fourth, fix the gates: N from a binomial bound (about 600 clean items for 0.5% at 95%), a value cap on auto-accepted lines, audit never below 5% for derived lines, and the top-80%-of-value rule kept as the primary control. Fifth, fix the schema before promising claims: add chainage to RW-* and EW-* rows, make it mandatory on DR-* rows, and measure the roll-up against the SO-certified pack rather than the QS draft. Sixth, keep a named QS as signatory on every bid, claim and certificate, notify the PI/CAR insurer of the AI-assisted process in writing given the AI exclusions now entering the market, and route any text extraction for LTA, HDB and PUB documents through a Singapore-resident or local model until a client has confirmed otherwise in writing. Seventh, hold the year-two automatic measurer budget behind a two-day untuned run of the existing extractor on ten real consultant plan sheets; if untuned precision is under half, the 15-20 person-week figure is a floor and the money is better spent on a DXF request letter and the DXF fast path.

verdicts.reasoning: Three engineering objections. (1) Statistics: 300 clean items with zero errors give a 95 percent upper bound of 1.0 percent (rule of three), not 0.5 percent; 600 clean items are needed for 0.5 percent at 95 percent and about 920 at 99 percent, and the probability of seeing 300 clean items when the true rate is 0.5 percent is 22 percent, so the gate cannot distinguish 0.5 from 1 percent. Golden tests catch engine regressions, not input or interpretation errors. (3) The 'clean' judgement in assist mode is the QS accepting engine output, which is exactly where automation bias lives (the digest cites 45 percent of assisted errors from over-reliance), so clean lines are not independent verifications unless blind. The digest itself says the 200-500 figure is a medical-coding heuristic, not a power calculation.

overall: The design depends most on four claims: C2 (preambles reduce to typed parameters), C5 (real Revu markups are readable into scaled primitives), C8 (DR Capture rows carry BQ-item keys) and C10 (a 0.3-0.5 FTE builder delivers the spine in six months). Each is weakened by specific evidence rather than by taste: the rulebook schema has no judgement-flag layer for rock, services, water and breaking-out clauses; the markup spike reads only what it wrote and ignores page-level /VP viewports and /Contents values that real Revu files use; DR Capture's depth bands (1.5/3/6 m) do not align with BQ bands (2/4/6 m), pipe sizes sit in free text and DR sums are the wrong operator for nett-measured excavation; and the person-week budget prices each spine component at five or six days that the more careful design prices at two to five weeks. The year-two automated primitives (C6, C7, C14) are further undermined by first-hand inspection of real LTA sheets in this session: up to 98,000 paths per page dominated by hatch strokes, pages with no extractable scale string, pen weights that change between editions of the same sheet, one clip box on multi-scale pages, and gradient labels that read as scales; item-level confidence calibration is statistically out of reach for most classes within a year and its dual-route check cannot see scale or classification errors. The statistical gate in C4 (300 clean lines) bounds error at 1 percent, not 0.5 percent, and counts correlated lines as independent. The sceptic would change the design as follows: (1) put the week-1 BQ line census, the three-contract preamble encoding with judgement flags, and the 20-real-PDF annotation dump ahead of any engine code, and let their results set scope; (2) drop the separate primitive capture app in favour of harvesting primitives from the QS's existing Excel dims sheets and real Revu markups, with the engine as a formula layer over what they already type; (3) make the claim roll-up a two-contract pilot built as drawing-quantity times chainage progress, adding BQ-item keys to DR Capture first; (4) reframe automated vector-PDF measurement as a pre-highlight assist overlay with two-click viewport calibration and DXF-on-request as the only auto-quantity route, budgeted at 30-40 person-weeks or deferred; (5) replace item-level confidence gating and the 300-line rule with tender- and sheet-level structural gates (at least 8-10 tenders per family, 600 blind-verified lines, QS-confirmed scale and legend per viewport) and a permanent audit sample; (6) make local-only text processing the default until the contracts person has written clearance per tier; and (7) commit only to the 6-month effort figure until the timer baseline and the two-QS agreement study exist.

overall: The design rests on four claims that are all human rather than technical: that the engine removes QS minutes instead of adding a typed-table double entry beside Bluebeam and Excel (C3); that foreman-filled DR rows are claim-grade on the fields that matter (C8, refuted on the app's own validation rules and its age); that one part-time builder can ship a canvas, engine, harvester, claims module and then an auto-measure stack (C10, refuted by arithmetic and the repo's own commit cadence); and that tender text may leave KKL at all (C9, a legal reading nobody has made). The effort curve (C11) is those claims multiplied together, minus governance hours the curve forgets. The sceptic would change the design as follows: make the QS's existing files the input, not a new app, by reading their trench workbooks and Bluebeam/Excel outputs and writing engine-vs-QS columns and BQ codes back into them; build the rules engine, rulebook with an explicit exceptions list and per-line audited overrides, and the BQ binder as the entire six-month scope; run the claims module as an evidence binder that attaches DR rows and tickets to the QS's lines and fixes DR Capture's fields first (chainage or fixed zone on every measured row, subcontractor quantities from delivery notes and weighbridge, not foreman estimates); default every contract to no-cloud until the contracts manager has read three NDAs in writing, and design the rulebook to be drafted from client templates by the chief QS so nothing depends on cloud extraction; defer vector auto-measure to a funded second builder or year three and push DXF and TrueType plot requests into every tender letter instead; replace the percentage effort curve and the QS-pressed timer with capacity metrics (tenders and claim packs per QS per month, days from drawings-in to quantity sheet, omissions caught) derived from file timestamps; budget the chief QS at one day a week explicitly with MD protection and the two-QS baseline shrunk to five sheets with a categorical disagreement column; and auto-accept only arithmetic, never inputs or measured primitives, until KKL has measured its own escaped-error baseline from last year's correspondence.
